title: The future of work
subtitle: Automation & artificial intelligence
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: Artificial intelligence and new forms of employment are shaking up a work model inherited from the industrial era.

hero.hook: Machines work faster than ever. It remains to be seen what will remain to be done to humans.

blocks.text: Work not only defines our income: it also shapes our social identity and the meaning we give to our days. However, artificial intelligence, robotics and new ways of working are today shaking up this model inherited from the industrial era.
This course explores how work changes shape, and the big questions that this transformation raises: fewer hours, more machines, and a new sharing of wealth.

sections.title: The end of the model born with Henry Ford

blocks.text: Modern work has long been organized around an idea popularized by , who established the 40-hour week in 1926. This choice was not a gesture of generosity: workers with free time also become customers, capable of buying the products they produce themselves. **[[Henry Ford]]**

In 1930, economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that his grandchildren would only work 15 hours a week, thanks to technological advances. Almost a century later, we have this technology, but we still work just as hard.

This model is crumbling today in favor of the **gig economy**, the “gig” economy: more than 57 million workers in the United States now sell their services via digital platforms, outside of traditional employment. Automation is also taking over increasingly complex tasks, while teleworking, accelerated by the 2020 pandemic, is reshaping the very geography of work.

sections.title: AI and the challenge of creative destruction

blocks.text: The debate on the future of work is often based on an idea from the philosopher and economist : the . According to him, each technological revolution destroys old professions, but ends up creating new ones, often more qualified. Generative artificial intelligence, however, introduces something new: it threatens, for the first time, office jobs and professions considered intellectual. **[[Joseph Schumpeter]]** **[[Creative destruction (Schumpeter)]]**
In 2023, a study showed that artificial intelligence performed better than 99% of humans on a creativity test, challenging the idea that creativity is our last advantage over machines.

Three scenarios are emerging. The optimist imagines an increase in productivity that would free humans from repetitive tasks. The pessimist fears that AI will advance faster than our ability to retrain, creating massive unemployment. Hybrid, finally, relies on collaboration between humans and machines, where the key skill would become the ability to direct the tools rather than mastering fixed know-how.

Faced with the risk of a two-speed society, new tools are being studied. The **universal basic income** proposes to pay a fixed sum to each citizen, without conditions, to secure life courses in an economy where work is becoming more intermittent.

blocks.caption: Automation, artificial intelligence and new forms of employment are reshaping the world of work.

blocks.text: In addition, the idea of ​​a **[[The 4-day week (32 hours)]]** is gaining ground: if machines produce more in less time, it seems logical that human working time should decrease in return, to maintain employment and preserve the health of workers. There remains a question of financing: if value is increasingly created by software, taxes will undoubtedly have to shift from labor income to capital income.

sections.title: What meaning to give to the work of tomorrow

blocks.text: Once the economic equation has been resolved, a deeper question remains: what becomes of the meaning of our days in a world where work is less central? Historically, work has structured daily life and self-esteem. Its partial disappearance could lead either to boredom or to a revival of voluntary, artistic or civic activities.
The word “work” comes from the Latin tripalium, a three-staked instrument of torture. An origin which reminds us that it was long perceived as suffering before becoming an identity.

In this context, learning to learn becomes an essential skill. The real issue is not only technological, but political: will we use artificial intelligence to increase our capabilities, or only to reduce business costs? The answer will determine whether tomorrow's work will be a liberation or a new constraint.

The future of work is marked by the end of single employees, in favor of the gig economy, and by the challenge of artificial intelligence, which threatens intellectual jobs for the first time. Our social model will undoubtedly have to redistribute productivity gains, through a universal income or a shorter working week.
